hypothesis: The lipid feature annotated as 'Latanoprost ethyl amide' (Esi+, m/z-RT 10.558985; METLIN 4571) is increased or characteristic in 5-month-old infants relative to 12-month-old infants.
rationale: No literature was found that reports this feature - or the named compound - in infant gut/stool, plasma metabolome, or in any age-comparison of 5- vs 12-month-old infants. All search results for 'latanoprost ethyl amide' (CAS 607351-44-0, Lat-NEt) were vendor/analytical-standard pages (Cayman, Biomol, GlpBio, MedChemExpress, Santa Cruz) describing it as a synthetic F-series prostaglandin analog in which the C-1 carboxyl of latanoprost is converted to an N-ethyl amide, developed as an ocular hypotensive prodrug for glaucoma; deuterated Lat-NEt-d4 exists purely as an LC-MS internal standard. It is not a known endogenous human metabolite, and unless the study infants were exposed to the drug (implausible), this annotation is almost certainly a library mis-assignment of an isobaric endogenous lipid - most plausibly an oxylipin/prostanoid-like or fatty-acid-amide species (C25H39NO4, MW 417.6, ESI+). Only generic, pathway-level reasoning can be offered in support of the hypothesized direction: prostaglandins E2 and F2alpha are present in human milk at concentrations reported to be far above adult plasma levels and are thought to modulate gastrointestinal physiology of breastfed infants (Pediatrics 1980; Am J Clin Nutr; Pediatr Res 1986), so a prostaglandin-F-like ESI+ feature could conceivably be higher during predominant milk feeding at 5 months than after the complementary-feeding transition at 12 months. Separately, primary work on the complementary-feeding transition (PLOS One 2022) and longitudinal formula/breastfed cohorts document substantial shifts in fecal lipid metabolites between ~6 and 12 months, establishing that age-related change in lipid features is expected - but neither addresses this feature. Because relevant but only indirect/theoretical material was located, and nothing directly tests this feature+group combination, this scores 1 (Weak) rather than 0 (nothing found) or 2.

evidence.title: Latanoprost ethyl amide (CAS 607351-44-0) - Cayman Chemical
evidence.study_population: Not a study; chemical vendor/reference entry
evidence.relevance: Establishes that the annotated compound is a synthetic latanoprost analog (F-series prostaglandin N-ethyl amide), i.e. a xenobiotic drug-like standard rather than a documented endogenous infant metabolite - the key caveat for interpreting this feature.

evidence.title: Latanoprost ethyl amide-d4 (Lat-NEt-d4) stable isotope standard
evidence.study_population: Not a study; analytical standard description
evidence.relevance: Confirms Lat-NEt is used chiefly as an LC-MS/GC-MS quantification standard and was introduced as an ocular hypotensive prodrug, supporting the interpretation that its presence in an infant lipidomics library reflects a spectral-library match rather than in vivo occurrence.

evidence.title: Prostaglandins in Human Milk (Pediatrics)
evidence.study_population: Six healthy nursing mothers delivering at term; foremilk/hindmilk across colostrum, transitional and mature milk
evidence.relevance: Primary measurement showing PGE2 and PGF2alpha are detectable in all human milk samples; provides the only (indirect, pathway-level) basis for expecting a prostaglandin-F-like species to be relatively higher during milk-dominant feeding at 5 months than at 12 months.

evidence.title: Prostaglandins in human milk (PubMed record)
evidence.study_population: Human breast milk versus adult plasma
evidence.relevance: Reports E- and F-series prostaglandins in milk at concentrations far exceeding adult plasma, corroborating milk as a dietary source of F-prostanoids to the young infant; still indirect for this feature and does not compare 5- vs 12-month infants.

evidence.title: Adaptation of the infant gut microbiome during the complementary feeding transition (PLOS One)
evidence.study_population: Human infants followed longitudinally through complementary feeding, including 9-12 months
evidence.relevance: Primary study documenting that fecal lipid metabolites shift markedly between 9 and 12 months in association with taxonomic change - shows age-dependent lipid features are plausible, but does not report this compound or its direction.

evidence.title: Longitudinal Profiles of Dietary and Microbial Metabolites in Formula- and Breastfed Infants (Front Mol Biosci)
evidence.study_population: Formula-fed and breastfed human infants over the first year of life
evidence.relevance: Reports that fecal metabolome differences tied to milk feeding converge by 12 months, consistent with milk-derived metabolites being relatively higher at earlier timepoints; indirect, feature not measured.

caveats: The annotation itself is the dominant caveat: 'Latanoprost ethyl amide' is a synthetic glaucoma prodrug/analytical standard with no established endogenous human occurrence, so a METLIN-based ESI+ match in infant samples is very likely an isobaric mis-annotation (C25H39NO4, 417.6 Da). Any biological interpretation should be deferred until MS/MS confirmation against an authentic standard and retention-time matching. The supporting prostaglandin-in-milk literature applies only if the true underlying ion is an F-prostanoid-like oxylipin, which is unverified. Also note that milk prostaglandin studies reported concentrations broadly stable across lactation stages, so even under that assumption the 5- vs 12-month contrast would be driven by feeding volume/weaning status rather than by milk composition per se, and no study directly tests this.
